title: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
description: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools h
body: For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025, external.Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go."You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break, external, essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean, external even broader job losses.Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.US tech workers are typically well-compensated, external, and while other industries such as investment banking, law and medicine also often see people work long hours, a 14-hour workday was not always the norm in tech. For years, it was a more typical 9-5 office job.But the former OpenAI employee said they would put in at least 70 hours a week, much more than they did in previous tech jobs. The person now works at a start-up also focused on AI, and said their work-life balance has improved, working closer to 50-60 hours a week, "outside of sprints".A "sprint" is term for a common period in technology companies in which people work long hours in the weeks leading up to a release of a new feature or product.Inside AI companies and larger tech companies working furiously on AI projects, however, such sprints can be extreme. At OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, sprints can stretch on for many weeks and top 90 hours of work in a seven-day period, tech workers that the BBC spoke to for this story said.Neither company responded to BBC requests for comment. At Meta, workers said they have been abruptly pushed onto teams this year doing AI work being treated as urgent. They called it being "drafted", according to one current and one former employee, because people were not given a choice."They just move you over," the former employee said. "You can't say no – or if you do, you have to quit."They said although Meta recently began to walk back, external that strict take it or leave us approach, by then many workers had already been forced onto such work.The hours on such teams at Meta are often long, with staff working into the night, on weekends, and feeling they are "on call" during the hours they are not working, according to descriptions of the work from the current and former employees.There are no limits, external in the US on how many hours a person over the age of 16 can work. In the UK and Europe, for instance, laws limit a working week to 48 hours, including overtime.Meta's current AI projects include the creation of an AI tool that can be used for software engineering and other kinds of work, and building AI model infrastructure that can measure an AI model's success in replicating various tasks, the employees added."You're literally working in teams of people trying to replicate humans doing jobs," the former employee said.That work, the person added, seems "endless".A Meta spokesperson declined to comment.Even tech workers who are not directly involved in the development of AI tools are facing longer hours due to the technology.A former Google employee, Amin Shali, left the company in May due to the ways in which he claimed AI was negatively impacting his job, like having to often work all hours of the night because internal engineering functions had failed. This was happening more frequently as Google moved crucial resources like processing units and memory storage over to AI projects.A Google spokesperson declined to comment.Since leaving Google, Shali told the BBC that his sleep and overall health had improved. He said he's realised that heavy reliance on AI tools in large tech companies "creates a bad culture with excess pressure on engineers".Some new research suggests that AI tools are making people's workloads even more burdensome.A study, external out of UC Berkeley followed hundreds of workers at a US tech company for eight months as they used AI. It found the employees "worked at a faster pace, took on a broader scope of tasks, and extended work into more hours of the day".Neil Thompson, an innovation scholar at MIT, said that even at tech companies leading on AI development, it is unlikely that workers are being told to simply deploy the tools that are supposed to do some of their work and move on."It leads to a situation where even if there were real time savings, it would be sucked up by the changes, and implementing them, and making sure they worked," Thompson said.The UC Berkeley research found that the workload of tech employees was expanded in part because of the need to constantly check the output of AI tools.In a situation where an employee had smoothed out processes for AI tools, people also tend to fill any time saved with more work, Thompson added, either because they want to or they feel they should do in order to prove their value to an employer."People assume that 20% less work means four-day weeks," Thompson said. "But new work emerges."As Shali observed: "AI is supposed to be doing so much for us now, so many more people should at least have better health and better sleep."Instead, it seems to be the opposite.

schema.headline: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week

title: Typhoon Dolphin: China evacuates more than 1 million people as massive storm arrives
description: Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon D
body: Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday.While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north.Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year.It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.Governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai.Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai, an area popular with tourists, and people wading through ankle-deep waters.Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties.Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say.Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters.Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou.In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects.The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. It also has a massive circulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported.

schema.headline: Typhoon Dolphin: China evacuates more than 1 million people as massive storm arrives

title: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss appears before Special Criminal Court
description: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradi
body: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extraditionImage source, SolarpixImage caption, Kinahan, pictured here in 2010, was extradited to the Republic of Ireland on SundayByGabija GataveckaiteDublin correspondentEimear Flanagan and Barry O'ConnorBBC News NISuspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has appeared before a Dublin court after being extradited from Dubai.He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.An Irish government jet carrying the 49-year-old landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival.Following a 13-minute non-jury hearing at the Special Criminal Court, he was remanded in custody until 5 October.Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful.The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan arrived into Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, Dublin on the government jet on Sunday eveningThe US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other members of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives.A large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing.Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk.Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said the arrest shows the force's determination to "target transnational organised crime groups" alongside international policing partners such as Dubai police.He added it shows the value of the force's relationship with the authorities in the UAE, the Irish ministry of justice at judicial level, and "on a police-to-police basis".'I won't be getting bail'Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A police convoy escorted Kinahan at speed to the courtKinahan arrived at Baldonnell Casement Aerodrome on Sunday evening, where gardaí arrested and charged him.He was directly transported under heavy police guard to the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin.All the benches were full in a packed courtroom of journalists, a number of solicitors from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), some members of the public and court clerks.In court, Kinahan was sitting on a wooden bench and wearing a black hooded top.He appeared before judges Patrick McGrath, Sarah Berkeley and Fiona Lydon, and rose to his feet when the three judges took their places.Image source, Mike O'DonnellImage caption, An artist's impression of Kinahan during his hearing on SundayKinahan did not have legal representation, and told the court that he did not have time to arrange this.When Judge McGrath suggested that he should be charged today and legal representation arranged later on, Kinahan replied: "If I have time, yes."Det Sgt Colm Davison told the court he arrested Kinahan earlier that evening.Judge McGrath asked Kinahan if he would like to appear at the next court sitting in person or via videolink.Kinahan asked if he had to "decide now" and it was explained to him he could make a decision later and notify the governor in the prison.Judge McGrath explained to Kinahan he could file an application for bail through the High Court.Kinahan replied: "I think we all know I won't be getting bail, but thank you for your time."'Landmark of judicial cooperation'The UAE and Ireland have an extradition treaty and on Sunday justice ministers from both jurisdictions issued a joint statement welcoming Kinahan's extradition."The Irish national is regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime and is accused of directing an organised crime organisation," it stated.Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan described the extradition as a "landmark of judicial cooperation between the two countries".He also commended "the professionalism, efficiency, and diligence demonstrated by the UAE judicial authorities throughout the extradition proceedings".His UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said it underscored "the steadfast commitment we have to supporting global efforts to combat transnational organised crime". The extradition agreement was previously used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan organised crime group.He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.What is the Kinahan cartel?According to former Garda Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£857,870,000) globally from its activities.The US Treasury Department has in the past compared the gang to crime organisations such as Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza.A reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) has also been offered by the US for information on Daniel, his father Christopher Snr and brother Christopher Jnr.Image source, CAROLINE QUINN/GETTY IMAGESImage caption, Gangland rivals tried to shoot Daniel Kinahan during a boxing weigh-in event in Dublin's Regency Hotel 10 years agoIn 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively.The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m.Kinahan himself became a target for murder and escaped an attempt on his life during a fatal shooting at a Dublin hotel in 2016.He left Ireland and spent time living in Spain and more recently in Dubai, where a warrant for his arrest was issued by the Irish courts in April. Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

schema.headline: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss appears before Special Criminal Court

title: Newspaper headlines: 'New prisons outrage' and 'Days of danger'
description: The government's chief post-Brexit negotiator tells the Guardian, external that the UK will "move faster" toward closer ties with Europe under Andy Bu
body: The government's chief post-Brexit negotiator tells the Guardian, external that the UK will "move faster" toward closer ties with Europe under Andy Burnham. Hamish Falconer says there's "room to be ambitious" within Labour's red lines on Europe, which exclude reopening discussions on the single market and customs union.Chinese spy cameras have been found on Royal Navy drones used by elite special forces, according to a report in the Daily Telegraph, external. It says components made in China were able to transmit data back to Beijing. The Ministry of Defence tells the paper there's no evidence any sensitive data or systems had been sent abroad.A report in the Times, external claims Prime Minister Andy Burnham is struggling to convince one of his closest allies to join his government because of differing opinions on wealth taxes. According to the paper, Lord O'Neill, a former Goldman Sachs economist and Treasury minister, has been offered significant roles but has previously said he is "very opposed" to wealth taxes because they could be "easily gamed".The Financial Times, external leads on claims from some former CIA officials, who've accused President Trump of following an "autocrat's playbook" and leaving the US "less safe". One tells the paper US democratic "guardrails" have been taken down and adds: "I don't think we're close to the worst of where we're going to". A White House official is quoted as saying Donald Trump puts "American citizens first".The Daily Mail, external, citing figures compiled by the Conservative Party, says 89,000 more crimes will be committed across Britain as a result of the government's prisoner early release scheme. "Sex offenders, robbers and arsonists will cause mayhem" reads its front page. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson dismisses the data as highly speculative and inaccurate.Car washes and private membership swimming pools could face water bans in the next heatwave according to the i Paper, external. It says some water firms are preparing "non-essential" restrictions for the first time in twenty years. The Daily Mirror, external focuses on warnings from bereaved families of the dangers of open water swimming during the hot weather.And the Metro, external leads on the prime minister bringing forward new rules to make it easier to cancel subscriptions. "Andy wants a cancel culture", reads its headline.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'New prisons outrage' and 'Days of danger'

title: The Hundred 2026 results: Sunrisers Leeds close to qualification after Welsh Fire win
description: The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleySunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Car
body: The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleySunrisers Leeds 201-4 (100 balls): Marsh 50 (34); Woakes 2-41Welsh Fire 130-6 (100 balls): Short 43 (29); Carse 3-24Sunrisers Leeds won by 71 runsScorecard. TableSunrisers Leeds moved closer to securing qualification for The Hundred's knockout stages with a comprehensive 71-run win over Welsh Fire.Mitch Marsh, the tournament's leading run-scorer, struck his fourth half-century of the season for second-placed Sunrisers as they made 201-4 at Headingley.The Australian opener hit a 34-ball 50 and added 89 for the first wicket with Ryan Rickelton.Chris Woakes, who took 2-41, claimed the breakthrough when he had Rickelton caught for 40, while Harry Brook (23 from 11 balls) and Marsh fell within the space of five deliveries, caught off Jordan Clark and Lockie Ferguson respectively.Captain Zak Crawley struck four sixes in a 12-ball 34 as Sunrisers pressed on, while Dan Lawrence (29) and Matthew Revis (15) ended the innings with an unbroken partnership of 27.Fifth-placed Fire were unable to keep up with the required run-rate in their reply as only Matt Short (43) and Joe Root (31), who put on 49 for the second wicket, made more than 13.Short was one of three victims for Brydon Carse, who also removed opener Phil Salt (13) and Marco Jansen (1).Root was caught behind off Nathan Ellis, who also bowled Rachin Ravindra for two, while Jordan Cox also fell cheaply, caught for 12 off Matthew Potts.Tom Kohler-Cadmore and Woakes both finished unbeaten on 13 as Fire closed on 130-6, well short of their target having chosen to chase at the toss.Sunrisers now only need to avoid defeat against Manchester Super Giants on Tuesday to progress, while victory would put them in contention for top spot should leaders Trent Rockets lose against Southern Brave on Monday.Fire, who would have moved second with a win on Sunday, are the lowest placed of three teams on 16 points and will likely need success against London Spirit on Wednesday and then rely on net run-rate to secure the final knockout spot.The Hundred men's competition, HeadingleyBirmingham Phoenix 162-4 (100 balls): Clarke 73 (42), Dickson 51 (28); Crocombe 1-8London Spirit 166-3 (82 balls): Livingstone 66 (30), Brevis 55 (31); Thompson 1-24London Spirit won by seven wicketsScorecard. TableDewald Brevis and Liam Livingstone shared a 103-run partnership as London Spirit beat Birmingham Phoenix by seven wickets at Lord's.In a match between two eliminated sides, Livingstone hit 66 from 30 balls, while Brevis struck an unbeaten 55 from 31 as Spirit passed their target of 163 with 18 balls to spare.Coming together at 43-2 after the hosts had lost Jonny Bairstow and Lhuan-dre Pretorius for 10 and 16 respectively, the pair struck a collective total of 12 fours and seven sixes, hitting the ball deep into the stands on multiple occasions.Home captain Livingstone skied a catch to Sean Dickson off Tom Helm, but Brevis saw Spirit home alongside James Coles (9), striking back-to-back fours to first reach his half-century and then end the match.Phoenix reached what appeared to be a competitive score after being put into bat, with opener Joe Clarke scoring 73 from 42 deliveries and Dickson hitting an unbeaten 51 from 28.The pair put on a third-wicket stand of 92 after Mitch Owen, Joe Weatherley and Laurie Evans had all fallen for single figures, while Clarke ultimately departed from the 91st ball of the innings, caught by Livingstone off Henry Crocombe.Phoenix's sixth defeat in seven matches mean they stay bottom of The Hundred standings, while Spirit moved level with sixth-placed Southern Brave on eight points, but remain beneath them by virtue of an inferior net run-rate.Nottingham is the venue for Monday's action in The Hundred with Trent Rockets hosting Southern Brave.The match for the women's side at 15:00 BST is a top-of-the-table clash, with leaders Rockets aiming to clinch their place in the Lord's final.Victory over Brave in their final match would secure their spot, although given they have a superior net run-rate they could go directly to Lord's even if they lose.Second-placed Brave are in a strong position to secure a place in the Eliminator - and would be certain if they win.The Rockets' men's side will also secure their spot in the final on 16 August with victory over Brave in their match which gets under way at 18:00.Brave are playing for pride, having already been eliminated and victory would guarantee they avoid the wooden spoon.You can follow ball-by-ball commentary on both matches on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

schema.headline: The Hundred 2026 results: Sunrisers Leeds close to qualification after Welsh Fire win

title: Jose Mourinho agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Man Utd in 2013
description: After years of speculation, Jose Mourinho has confirmed he agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United, before changing his mind and rejo
body: After years of speculation, Jose Mourinho has confirmed he agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United, before changing his mind and rejoining Chelsea instead.When Ferguson retired in 2013 after 26 years at Old Trafford, he recommended then Everton manager David Moyes be appointed as his successor.That led to Moyes being labelled 'The Chosen One' - including on a banner that hung at the Stretford End of the club's stadium.Speaking in a new documentary series about his career, which is on Netflix from 11 August, Mourinho said: "When I left Real Madrid, I signed to go to Manchester United after Sir Alex.Ferguson, who won 13 Premier League titles as United manager, confirmed Mourinho was "offered the job"."I sat him down and explained the situation," he added. "As far as I was concerned, he was accepting. And then, within hours, it changed."What changed was that Mourinho felt he could not turn down a return to Chelsea, where he had won consecutive Premier League titles in 2005 and 2006.Ferguson said: "One night, he phoned me and he was crying and he says: 'Alex, I can't take it. I've given my word to Chelsea and I'm not going to break my word.'"The reason he gave to me, I could understand, but I was disappointed."Mourinho, 63, said he was "very flattered" to be offered the job of replacing Ferguson "because Manchester United has an incredible appeal"."But one thing is love for football, another thing is love for a certain club," he explained."I think this is more powerful than love for football and fundamentally, after Real Madrid, I needed to feel that I'm loved."For me to lose the chance to be the coach to succeed Sir Alex Ferguson was dramatic, but I don't regret [it] because it was a decision that I made with my heart."After returning to Stamford Bridge in 2013, Mourinho went on to win his third Premier League title as well as the League Cup.Moyes, meanwhile, was sacked after just 10 months as United manager.Mourinho accepted a second chance to take over at Old Trafford in 2016, succeeding Louis van Gaal.Over a two-and-a-half-year spell at Old Trafford, Mourinho won League Cup and Europa League titles before being sacked in December 2018 following a slump in results.After taking over a struggling Real side, Mourinho helped them challenge the dominance of Pep Guardiola's Barcelona, winning La Liga, Copa del Rey and Spanish Super Cup trophies in his first two seasons at the Bernabeu. The 100 points they amassed in 2011-12 remains unsurpassed in La Liga history.However, the wheels came off in Mourinho's third season in the Spanish capital and he was dismissed at the end of 2012-13 with his side finishing 15 points behind rivals Barcelona, who matched Real's 100-point record.Mourinho's treatment of Casillas divided the dressing room. The goalkeeper made 725 appearances across 25 years at Real, winning three Champions League titles and five La Liga crowns, but had spent much of the 2012-13 season on the bench."The relationship Jose and I had was very cold," Casillas said. "In those years, I really think it was taken to a limit where in the end, the rope broke."Former Real midfielder Sami Khedira said Mourinho's rift with Casillas affected everyone."Iker is a Real Madrid legend, loved by every Real Madrid supporter. He benched him, doesn't speak to him, spoke bad about him in the media, so then this locker room was a nightmare, honestly," he said."After that, the relationship between Jose and many, many players was broken - like Cristiano [Ronaldo] and the Spanish guys, Casillas, Sergio Ramos. And those players were super, super important for the atmosphere in the locker room."Mourinho claimed that the keeper had a bad attitude."The first three times that I spoke to Casillas, the captain, the first thing he told me was, 'I want to ask for more holidays for the national team players'," Mourinho said."The second time he spoke to me was, 'I would like to ask you to put the training sessions one hour later because at the time you want the training sessions, there is a lot of traffic in Madrid'. The third time he comes to speak with me was, 'We don't want to go to [the] hotel. We prefer just to meet on matchday and go direct to the stadium to play'. And in a short period of time, I realised they're spoilt."Former Spain captain Casillas also revealed that he clashed with Mourinho over the manager's attitude towards his international team-mates who played for Barcelona.The 63-year-old's response was unapologetic.Mourinho said: "There are things that I don't accept and I will never accept and when somebody doesn't respect me, it's a problem. I say, this is Barcelona, Real Madrid. When you go to the national team, then you can kiss the guy, but not now. This is war."Mourinho was sacked by Abramovich at Chelsea in 2007 and 2015.The veteran manager said that his former boss became increasingly interfering during his first spell at the club, including pushing for the signing of Andriy Shevchenko.The Ukraine striker joined Chelsea in May 2006 for a then club record fee of approximately £30m, but scored only nine league goals in 48 games over a three-year spell in West London."Abramovich - incredible passion for football, but knowing nothing about the situation," Mourinho said on the new documentary."Shevchenko was on the table because of connections with the boss, connections with agents and I never wanted to sign him, but I never told no-one, so it's also my responsibility. You want to know the player that I wanted? [Samuel] Eto'o."Following his dismissal by the Russian oligarch in September 2007, Mourinho had a chance for revenge when he returned to Stamford Bridge in March 2010 with Inter Milan in the last 16 of the Champions League. The Italian side beat Chelsea 1-0 on the night and 3-1 on aggregate, in a season when they went on to lift the trophy."Honestly, I was playing against Roman that game," Mourinho said."I was playing against a guy that sacked me. I go home happy and he goes home upset. Because I know how much he loved Chelsea, I know how much he loves to win."But I needed revenge, because football belongs to people like me. The other ones are the intruders that don't belong. Football belongs to the players, belongs to the coaches, belongs to the fans. Football will always belong to us."

schema.headline: Jose Mourinho agreed to replace Sir Alex Ferguson at Man Utd in 2013

title: The Canadians taking fighting wildfires into their own hands
description: When a wildfire broke out near his First Nation community in northern Ontario, Hubert Wigwas decided to stay put.He put sprinklers on his roof to exti
body: When a wildfire broke out near his First Nation community in northern Ontario, Hubert Wigwas decided to stay put.He put sprinklers on his roof to extinguish falling embers. He checked on elders in his community who also stayed behind, and he fuelled up four boats down on the lake in case they needed a quick escape."This is everything I've built in my 58 years," Wigwas, a councillor from Gull Bay First Nation, told the BBC. "I'm just not going to run away and let it burn."Canada has seen some of its worst fire seasons in recent years, and experienced its most destructive on record in 2023, when blazes tore through forest land roughly the size of Syria. As of this August, more than 750 wildfires are actively burning across the country.The impact has been felt as far as the US Midwest, where smoke had choked the air in cities. Even President Donald Trump has taken note, threatening to further tariff Canada for allowing "filthy, polluted" air to waft south of the border.The intensifying wildfires have sparked a national conversation: Are there enough firefighters to battle these more challenging fire seasons? What happens when resources are stretched too thin? And how can remote communities, often closest to danger because of their proximity to Canada's vast boreal forest, learn to live with this new reality?Wigwas asked himself these questions when he decided to stay, even as he faces a fine of around C$800 ($570; £425) for defying evacuation orders.Leaders of Gull Bay First Nation, also known as Kiashke Zaaging Anishinaabek, have been urging residents to stay away since mid-July as more than 150 wildfires burn across Ontario's northwest.Its chief penned a letter on 29 July pleading with those who have remained to leave immediately, saying that Ontario firefighters cannot do their jobs safely with people still in their homes.It is the same message officials across the country have been conveying in British Columbia, where around 115 fires are currently burning. But with a wildfire 24km outside his community, Wigwas, speaking in late July, said he had yet to see fire personnel from out of town there to help fireproof properties or keep an eye out on the elders who remained.He said it made him realise that his First Nation would benefit from setting up its own wildfire emergency response and teaching residents how to protect their own homes."Everybody talks about climate change, but nobody is doing something to unite the (First Nations) reserves and have a system like that set up," Wigwas said.Dave Bradley, a spokesperson for Ontario's ministry of natural resources, did not address Wigwas' claim directly, but said the province has been in "constant contact" with First Nations leaders. He added that fire fighting resources are directed based on "fire behaviour, weather conditions and risks to communities."In the west-coast province of British Columbia - long the front line of Canada's wildfire response - people are doing just what Wigwas is envisioning for his First Nation, with efforts underway to train residents of rural and remote communities how to safely respond to wildfires before out-of-town crews can arrive.Sonja Leverkus, a wildfire researcher and specialist, said she has helped train more than 400 people in and around her community of Fort Nelson over the last three years through a firefighting group she helped start called the Northeast BC Rural Incident Management Team.She told the BBC that her efforts are inspired by a realisation that Canada needs to change how it fights wildfires as climate change increases their frequency and intensity."There are not enough human beings in Canada," she said, with the appropriate training, "to fight the fires that we have currently, especially over the last five years".Remote communities, where the nearest town might be hundreds of kilometres away, can sometimes be bumped down the priority list for BC firefighting crews if there are blazes threatening more populated areas, she said.Her crew, who are primarily indigenous, have carried out prescribed burns, also known as a hazard reduction burns – a practice of setting planned, controlled blazes to remove fuels that could contribute to wildfires.They have also helped put out smaller fires before they grow out of control using fire wagons that they purchased through fundraising and grants, sometimes arriving ahead of provincial firecrews and then working in tandem with them, Leverkus said.When a major wildfire tore through Fort Nelson in 2024, she said she and 40 of her team members stayed behind and were hired by the province to clear flammables and support fire suppression activities.Leverkus also organised a structural protection training course for locals to learn how to shield buildings from embers that can quickly spur fires that engulf entire towns."We have mechanics, we have carpenters, we have real good problem solvers," Leverkus said. "We're all not afraid to stay."Cam Allen, a 70-year-old former helicopter pilot in Fort Nelson who has previously fought fires from the air, said he recently took Leverkus' course to learn about ground fire suppression techniques, and, more broadly, how to help if a blaze reaches his town.He mentioned John Carr, a California man who went viral last year, external for staying behind and warding off flames with a garden hose during the Palisades fire, ultimately saving his home even when others around it burned down."It makes you wonder, if 100 people had stayed or 1,000 people had stayed behind and actually did what he did, how much more could have been saved?" Allen asked.But not all were as fortunate as Carr during the Los Angeles fires, which killed a total of 29 people – a few of whom had, too, defied evacuation orders in order to protect their homes, even as officials urged thousands in the area to leave.Leverkus' group is not officially recognised by BC's government, and what it is trying to achieve highlights simmering tensions in fire-prone regions between those who enforce evacuation orders and those who defy them.Last week, wildfire crews in BC were forced to rescue a man when his home in the Village of Clinton was surrounded by flames, after he had refused to evacuate. In a wildfire update on Tuesday, BC's minister responsible for emergency management reiterated that all those who are under evacuation orders should leave."We may not be able to get back to you if an emergency happens," warned Minister Kelly Greene, adding that evacuation orders are made as "a last resort to keep people and communities safe".Paul Kovacs, a researcher at the University of Western Ontario and director of its Catastrophic Loss Reduction Institute, said that Canada has had a lower fatality rate from wildfires despite their frequency in part because of its evacuation approach.The stay and defend mindset, he said, "is aggressively opposed" by the academic community in Canada, as opposed to other fire-prone countries like Australia."In the hierarchy of what is it that you do to manage a wildfire, preservation of life is first," Kovacs said.Rural and remote communities can and should play an outsized role in informing officials of how best to protect their town, he said, and can do a lot of work to fire proof homes and structures. But that work, he argued, should not be done "while the fire is burning."A spokesperson for BC's Ministry of Forests told the BBC that self-organised groups in rural areas can be hired temporarily by the province during an active wildfire, but only when there are no more available provincial firefighters in the area.The ministry added that BC Wildfire's full-time staff has increased by 56% in recent years to respond to the growing frequency of fires, in addition to seasonal staff.Leverkus said she has been exploring ways to have her programme recognised by BC officials so that those trained through it can also help without being penalised for staying behind.She added that safety precautions are engrained in her courses, including training on how to predict fire behaviour and mapping out at least two safe escape routes.Not all of those who are trained want to stay back, she said, but those that do receive orders from trained crew commanders, including on when it's time to leave."If people want to stay and defend, they need to understand what that means for themselves, what that means for their family," Leverkus said.Her goal is for the programme to one day become a blueprint that can be adopted by rural and remote communities across Canada, creating teams that can be relied on across the country.As for Wigwas, he will be fighting his evacuation fine in court."If the chief and council want to charge me for saving my house, and I end up with nowhere to live, I might as well be in jail," he said.

schema.headline: The Canadians taking fighting wildfires into their own hands

title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
description: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on
body: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers -  the case that Mathipa had been investigating.After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.Outside the UK watch on YouTube, externalThe case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer."When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.

schema.headline: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC

title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
description: Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightene
body: Lucy said she was staying at the hotel in London in October 2025 for "a night away from the fear" following a period of abuse that left her "frightened and exhausted"."He walked into the hotel and told the receptionist that his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. He asked what room I was in and what floor I was staying on," she said.The receptionist handed him a key before directing him upstairs to Lucy's room, she said."I couldn't believe it. The one place I thought he could never get to, he had somehow reached. I felt sick with panic. My safe place disappeared in an instant," she added.She said he physically attacked her and tried to grab her phone.After Lucy convinced her attacker to leave, he returned, "banging, shouting and becoming more aggressive"."I was absolutely terrified. I froze, hoping he would stop. Instead, he kicked the hotel room door off its hinges and forced his way back inside."Travelodge rooms have internal dead-bolt locks on the doors as well as electric key-card operated locks which can be opened from the outside.Lucy said she ran downstairs "shaking, crying and begging for help", adding: "I thought someone would protect me."Instead, Lucy was offered another room in the hotel.Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help."It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable."We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently."We went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Andy Smith said."I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It beggars belief."Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".A spokesperson for industry group UKHospitality said recent incidents were "extremely serious" and it understood the concerns from guests.It was working with its members to create guidance on customer security which would be published shortly, the spokesperson said."Developed with sector experts, we have continued to engage with ministers on this important work and received positive feedback from government on the work taking place to further bolster guest security," they said.After the Maidenhead sentencing, Travelodge said it had commissioned an independent review led by a barrister "to examine our room access security policies and escalation procedures"."While the independent review is progressing, we have also conducted an internal review and have since made changes to our room access security policy and incident escalation procedures supported by training for all of our customer-facing colleagues."Lucy said the night of her attack had "changed me forever", and she was now unable to stay in hotels because of the fear and anxiety she feels."Hotels need safeguarding procedures... because one mistake can have devastating consequences," she said.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

schema.headline: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room

title: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules
description: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says
body: A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear – plus a tie for secondary schools.Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.The government says the changes will save some families "up to £50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was £101.94 with a pinafore, and £83.95 without – but this year it will cost families an average of £53.97. Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms. Because every school sets its own uniform policy, parents can still face very different expectations and costs.Lorraine, who lives in London, has two children in secondary schools and is frustrated that her school has not changed any of its uniform policy this year.She says several items are still compulsory, including the branded blazer, tie, branded polo shirt, branded shorts and two-toned PE socks.Even the plain grey trousers or skirt have to be purchased from one of the school's suppliers, she says.Both her sons have been through a growth spurt this summer, so she is expecting to spend more than £200 on their branded items alone."I'm just frustrated, for me it's not even about the money," she says."I feel these inconsistencies do not make a difference to education and are really blinkered."But mum-of-five Carol, from Stockport, welcomes the changes at her children's school. She says her son's secondary school only requires a branded blazer, a branded jumper and tie, with everything else available from a range of shops.She tries to get most of her children's uniforms second-hand anyway, but always buys the blazer, which costs around £30, as she likes them to have a new one.She says anything that makes it more affordable for parents is a good thing.But others are not seeing the changes they would like.One father from Oxfordshire, who did not want to be named, says his daughter still has to have seven branded items - three for the uniform, three for PE and a summer polo shirt - as there are no alternatives allowed. "It's ridiculous and unfair. We are paying £200 which we can't afford," he says.Most primary schools already have very few branded items.At Broadhurst Primary, in North Manchester, only the school jumper – and, from 2027, the PE T-shirt – are branded, which the school says brings the total cost of its uniform to £13 per child.Around 23% of secondary schools will have to change their uniform lists for September to comply with the new rules, according to the latest government survey.The education secretary has legal powers to direct schools to comply if they are not sticking to the new rules.One head teachers' union, the Association of School and College Leaders, says the actual difference in cost is likely to be marginal for most families.Its general secretary Pepe Di'Iasio says schools are already trying to balance the cost to parents with maintaining a sense of identity. He says it's also important to keep expensive fashion brands out so no one feels excluded.Some schools have been phasing their changes in over the last few years.King's Oak Academy, in Bristol, has one compulsory item left on its uniform list - a branded PE T-shirt.The school, which goes from reception right through to Year 11, used to have a branded jumper, tie and a shirt, which together cost about £41.Students are now asked to wear a plain polo shirt - which changes colour for the lower, middle and upper school - a sweatshirt or cardigan, and grey skirt or trousers, with all pupils also wearing black trainers. The school says it now costs about £10 to £25, depending on where parents buy the uniform.

schema.headline: How much parents could save from September's new school uniform rules

title: Andoni Iraola: What we have learned from Liverpool's start under new boss
description: Winning is important - but for many fans, how a team plays in the hunt for wins is almost as significant.When results don't come, a style that fans en
body: Winning is important - but for many fans, how a team plays in the hunt for wins is almost as significant.When results don't come, a style that fans enjoy watching often buys a manager more time than a pragmatist might be afforded.Andoni Iraola replaced Arne Slot as Liverpool head coach a season after the latter won the Premier League with the Reds.Many believe the Spanish coach's style is more aligned with the 'heavy metal' style of football Anfield had come to love under Jurgen Klopp.So how have Liverpool fared in their pre-season games so far under Iraola?Liverpool have beaten Sunderland and Wrexham in pre-season, but they threw away two-goal leads in defeats by both Leeds and Monaco.They averaged 60.6% possession over this small sample size - which is a 12.9% jump on Bournemouth's average possession under Iraola in the league last season.With teams more likely to sit deep against Liverpool, having lots of possession is a newer challenge Iraola has to tackle.And he has looked to do this while sticking to the intense and chaotic style that typified his previous sides.Since joining Liverpool, many of Iraola's tactics in possession look as they did last season.Liverpool have looked to build up short at times with their goalkeeper, four defenders and one or two central midfielders deep.Dominik Szoboszlai and Trey Nyoni, Liverpool's preferred deeper midfield duo in pre-season, drop to show for the ball, bouncing it towards wide players in space.Iraola's sides have become known for fast and vertical counter-attacks but, with Liverpool looking to hold the ball more deliberately, these short passes in build-up are designed to entice opposition pressure before accelerating play.Once a team have committed players to pressing Liverpool, Iraola's men look for forward passes readily - almost manufacturing their own counter-attacks.If a team press immediately, Liverpool have been willing to skip short build-up play and go long from keepers Alisson or Giorgi Mamardashvili early.By playing directly, even if Liverpool lose the initial duel, they are well placed to pounce upon second balls. They then look to attack the spaces that open up centrally against disorganised defences.Many of Iraola's attacking principles resemble those of one of his long-time managerial inspirations, the former Leeds United boss Marcelo Bielsa.The Argentine coached Iraola at Athletic Club between 2011 and 2013 and, speaking to Sky Sports in 2023, the Liverpool boss acknowledged this influence."I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him, especially with the ball," Iraola said."Offensively, his teams are very dynamic, willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder offensively."Like Bielsa's sides, Iraola already has the Reds playing in a busy manner. When attacking, it is rare to see Liverpool's players filling specific areas in a rigid style.Another tactic Bielsa leans on is the use of wide pairings or trios to break teams down. Iraola experienced this at first hand when playing as a right-back for him.The full-back and winger would regularly combine on the outside, but the relationship was never as simple as one holding the width and the other supporting underneath statically.Bielsa, like Iraola now, encouraged players to change their positions in relation to each other.The winger could come inside, opening the outside lane for the full-back, while a midfielder would move towards the pair to create a third passing option.On other occasions, the full-back could move inside himself, allowing the winger to remain high and wide.Liverpool are already showing similar patterns under Iraola, especially on the left, where full-backs have pushed into the final third alongside Rio Ngumoha or Cody Gakpo on the left wing.Florian Wirtz, playing primarily as Liverpool's number 10 under Iraola, has drifted to that flank to provide a third option capable of playing centrally, deep or out wide.The rotations of these wide triangles make it hard for opponents to know who they should be picking up.By simplifying the attacking game into two-v-two or three-v-three situations, Liverpool are hoping to have a repeatable and dynamic solution, resulting in crosses from dangerous positions close to goal.As exciting as this style of play can appear, it does leave Liverpool very top-heavy.In the opening games, we have seen both full-backs join the attack alongside two of the midfield three and the front three.This can result in situations that leave only the two centre-backs and one holding midfielder positioned behind the ball, leaving Liverpool vulnerable to counter-attacks.Interestingly, Slot’s Liverpool were noticeably vulnerable against fast counter-attacks last season too.Iraola has spoken about the need for more control while retaining the chaos that makes his team's attacks so effective, so he may decide to leave additional players behind the ball as the season progresses.However, based off his previous principles and his managerial references, this feels less likely - with the Basque coach often encouraging six or seven players to push forward, leaving three or four players back when in attack.The hope is to stop counter-attacks being conceded at source through intense counter-presses, something that is helped by attacking down the sides and with extra bodies nearby to apply pressure.This is easier said than done at this early stage.Indeed, Iraola reflected on the loss to Monaco, saying his side "can't sustain the level we want, we have work to do", referring to the dropped leads in second halves, caused by a lack of depth, a drop-off in physicality, and a press that hasn't yet been perfected.Throughout pre-season, we have also seen Iraola's trademark high press. What stands out is the roles Liverpool's players are taking up and what that tells us about how he wants his side to defend.Szoboszlai played across the front line, midfield and even at right-back last season, but Iraola has mainly used him as the second central midfielder - a crucial role defensively.Liverpool have often pressed in a 4-4-2 diamond shape, initially encouraging opponents to play short before launching more aggressive pressing sequences, often funnelling the ball centrally before trying to win it back.One principle carried over from Iraola's Bournemouth side is looking to keep a spare defender against the opposition attack. If an opponent leaves three forwards high, Liverpool will commonly opt to keep four defenders back.That leaves one fewer player higher up the pitch, so Liverpool have to compensate through intensity and intelligent covering.When one player leaves his opponent to press somebody else, team-mates behind him have to recognise the movement and cover the player left free.This makes Szoboszlai's midfield role particularly important. When he jumps forward to press, the holding midfielder and defensive line have to react behind him or gaps can quickly appear."He is very good," the Hungary captain has said of his new manager. "The intensity we need is here now, what we have been missing is back."Szoboszlai's physicality allows him to cover the ground needed to make Liverpool's press feel numerically equal, while his judgement of when to step forward has helped the Reds start to implement Iraola's defensive ideas quickly.Image gallery 2Skip image galleryImage caption, Alexander Isak pressed the left centre-back of Leeds on the ball. Florian Wirtz is covering one of the central midfielders, Ethan Ampadu, but is looking to step up to apply pressure to the right centre-back. Dominik Szoboszlai is marking the other central midfielder, Ao Tanaka.Slide 1 of 3, Image showing Liverpool's press against Leeds in pre-season., Alexander Isak pressed the left centre-back of Leeds on the ball. Florian Wirtz is covering one of the central midfielders, Ethan Ampadu, but is looking to step up to apply pressure to the right centre-back. Dominik Szoboszlai is marking the other central midfielder, Ao Tanaka.

title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
description: The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS. Healthwa
body: The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS. Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill. The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished. The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety. The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal – where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths. A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal – one of the biggest in NHS history – involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008. Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.The NHS Modernisation Bill is currently at the report stage and due for a third reading on 7 September. Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan said this was "a catastrophic step backwards" and described it as the "greatest backward step in patient safety in a generation". "Andy Burnham must urgently put an end to this, and fix the Health Bill so that modernising the NHS doesn't come at the expense of accountability, transparency or patient safety," Morgan added.In a speech on NHS reform in January, then-Health Secretary Wes Streeting said "there are many decent people working at Healthwatch who care, but the job of listening to patients can't be farmed out to an arm's length body". "It must be core business for the NHS. That is why we're taking it back in-house and I won't back down on that either." The Lib Dems also said the current bill removes the duty for the NHS to cooperate with the Care Quality Commission in providing key safety data and removes automatic "safe space" protections for whistleblowers. Amendments tabled by the Liberal Democrats would cancel the changes and the party is "urging the new Burnham administration to adopt them".The party vowed to robustly fight the government in the House of Lords, where Labour doesn't have a majority.A DHSC spokesperson said NHS Modernisation Bill "explicitly preserves safe space provisions and staff will continue to be protected"."The reforms we are introducing will give patients a stronger, clearer voice at the heart of health and social care." Burnham was health secretary in 2009, when the Healthcare Commission's report was released on the Stafford Hospital scandal. Burnham then launched an independent inquiry in 2010.In May, the Local Government Association (LGA) told the BBC disbanding Healthwatch would be a "significant step back" in accountability."Without an independent, locally rooted voice to challenge and represent communities, there is a risk of duplication and gaps in accountability," the LGA said. There are currently more than 150 local Healthwatch organisations in England.

schema.headline: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say

title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happ
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, a senior Board of Peace official insisted the US-backed peace plan for the territory remained the only way forward.Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October."Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased.Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward. "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome".The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas.Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead".He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm.According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Additional reporting by Jack Burgess

schema.headline: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
